newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain probes ETA links to drugs, prostitution.
newsitem.headline: Spain probes ETA links to drugs, prostitution.

text.p: Spanish authorities are investigating possible links between the Basque guerrilla group ETA and drug trafficking, prostitution and money laundering, an Interior Ministry official said on Monday.

The police and Civil Guard may have new clues on how ETA finances its operations after the arrest last month of four separatist rebels who held Spanish prison worker Jose Antonio Ortega Lara hostage for a year and a half.
"One of those detained when Ortega Lara was freed had a number of businesses linked to money laundering," the Interior Ministry official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja, in a weekend interview with the Spanish news agency Europa Press, called ETA a mafia which functions like other organised crime networks.
"The markets where ETA has to do its buying probably means involvement in more than one business related to prostitution, money laundering and drugs," Mayor Oreja was quoted as saying.
ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) has come under intensified scrutiny recently following its killing of Basque town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco last month.
An estimated six million Spaniards took to the streets to demonstrate against ETA, which has killed more than 800 people in a 29-year campaign for an independent Basque state.
The police and Civil Guard have been trying for years to dismantle the group's financial network.

The Spanish daily El Pais reported on Monday that authorities were investigating businesses run by Emilio Arrizabalaga Ruiz de Azua, one of four ETA commandos who held Ortega Lara captive in a tiny, damp cell for 532 days. The newspaper said Arrizabalaga had various investments in real estate in Spain's southern Andalusia region.
ETA is believed to obtain a significant portion of its funds from a "revolutionary tax" which it forces wealthy businessmen in the Basque region to pay.
The group has also received large ransom payments for kidnapped businessmen.
The family of businessman Cosme Delclaux, released by ETA in July after eight months in captivity, paid about seven million dollars for his release, according to police sources.
